items.title: OFAC designates two Iranian-linked digital asset exchanges, Shelbit and Aban Tether, with crypto addresses on the SDN entries
items.content_text:
On August 7, 2026 the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced that OFAC "is moving against digital asset exchanges that the Iranian regime relies on to launder billions of dollars, maintain covert access to international financial systems, and support the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), among other terrorist groups." Treasury states the action targets two major digital asset exchanges used by Tehran along with the ringleader of a multi-jurisdiction front-company network. Siavash Kayvanpour, who operates Republic of Georgia-based SHPS Shelbit and the Shelbit Exchange, is designated under Executive Order 13224, as amended; Treasury states that digital currency addresses belonging to the IRGC sent the equivalent of over $1 million in digital assets to Shelbit Exchange addresses, that more than the equivalent of $2 million was transferred from Shelbit Exchange addresses to IRGC addresses, and that addresses controlled by Kayvanpour sent over $2 million in digital assets to U.S.-designated Nobitex. Also designated under E.O. 13224 are UAE-based Shelbit General Trading LLC, Poland-based Shelbit Technologies Ltd, and UAE-based Crypto Home DMCC and NFT Home DMCC. Iran-based Aban Tether, which Treasury states has processed millions of dollars' worth of transactions involving previously designated Iranian digital asset exchanges including Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin and Ramzinex, is designated under E.O. 13902. The corresponding SDN listing (OFAC recent action 20260807) records Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, BNB and Solana addresses across the Kayvanpour, SHPS Shelbit and Crypto Home DMCC entries, and marks the E.O. 13224 entries as carrying secondary sanctions risk under section 1(b) of E.O. 13224, as amended by E.O. 13886. Treasury states that all property and interests in property of the designated persons in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC, that entities owned 50 percent or more by blocked persons are also blocked, and that OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. Treasury points to FAQ 1250 and amended FAQ 1257 for sanctions risk associated with Iranian digital asset exchanges, including secondary sanctions risk, and states the action was developed in coordination with IRS-Criminal Investigation.

Primary source: U.S. Department of the Treasury press release sb0598, August 7, 2026 (SDN listing: OFAC recent action 20260807) — https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0598

items.title: OFAC designates Dubai exchange-house fronts and Hong Kong and Singapore shell companies in its eighth 2026 action against Iran's shadow banking networks
items.content_text:
On August 7, 2026 the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced that OFAC "took action against multiple networks spanning several countries for enabling Iran's rahbar banking system to move hundreds of millions of dollars," pursuant to Executive Order 13902. Treasury states this is OFAC's eighth action in 2026 targeting Iran's shadow banking apparatus. Per the release, Iran's Shahr Bank relies on two Dubai-based exchange house fronts, Titan Exchange (also operating as Titan Land Petrochemicals Trading L.L.C and Titan Energy Petroleum Products Trading Co. L.L.C) and Alps International L.L.C-FZ, and Titan Exchange held tens of millions of dollars on behalf of Shahr Bank as of early 2026. Treasury states that rahbar company Farab Soroush Afagh Qeshm operates an illicit payment network to facilitate transactions with China- and UAE-based shell companies, that a UAE-based team identified as the "Safe Group" carries out funds transfers and handles documentation for Chinese shell companies receiving money through intermediary accounts, and that in 2026 Alps International enabled hundreds of millions of dollars of transactions in multiple currencies. Designated individuals include Shahr Bank employee Saeed Ghasempour, FSAQ employees Shima Sharifi and Peivand Mohammad, and information technology specialist Amir Hendi. Designated entities include Hong Kong-based Oviedo Overseas Company Limited, Blue Dash General Trading Company Limited and Gleaming HK Trading Limited, Singapore-based Cailafang Pte. Ltd., and Dubai-based Aydeniz General Trading L.L.C. OFAC separately designated Basheer Abdulkadhim Alwan al-Shabbani under E.O. 13224, as amended. Treasury states that engaging in certain transactions involving the persons designated may risk the imposition of secondary sanctions on participating foreign financial institutions, and that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining a U.S. correspondent account or payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly facilitates significant transactions for a designated person.

items.title: FinCEN renews the Minnesota fraud Geographic Targeting Order covering banks and money transmitters in Hennepin and Ramsey Counties
items.content_text:
On August 7, 2026 the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced that FinCEN renewed its Geographic Targeting Order (GTO) "designed to combat fraud in Minnesota and protect U.S. taxpayers." Treasury states that the GTO "requires banks and money transmitters located in Hennepin and Ramsey Counties in Minnesota to report additional information about funds transfers of $3,000 or more to beneficiaries, recipients, or banks outside of the United States," and that "The terms of this GTO are effective for 180 days after publication on the Federal Register." Treasury further states that on February 27, 2026 FinCEN issued an order exempting a subset of banks from the GTO's requirement to record or report funds transfers where the originator falls into certain categories, that this exemption has been incorporated into the renewed GTO, and that the reporting requirements are otherwise unchanged from those in the February 2026 GTO. Treasury describes the underlying conduct as extensive schemes that fraudulently diverted state and Federal dollars intended for people who lack housing, are food insecure, have disabilities, or are otherwise eligible to receive government benefits, costing Minnesota potentially billions of dollars, a portion of which was laundered overseas. The release links the renewed order, a frequently asked questions document, a submission template and a template dictionary on fincen.gov.

items.title: FinCEN's renewed Minnesota Geographic Targeting Order is effective August 11, 2026 and ends February 6, 2027, and requires money transmitters to report whether a transmittal was a convertible virtual currency transmission
items.content_text:
The order document "Geographic Targeting Order Imposing Recordkeeping and Reporting Requirements on Certain Financial Institutions in Minnesota" (31 CFR Part 1010), signed by FinCEN Deputy Director Jimmy L. Kirby, states: "DATES: Effective Date: This action is effective on August 11, 2026," and "The terms of this Order are effective on August 11, 2026, and end on February 6, 2027." A "Covered Business" is "any bank, as defined in 31 CFR 1010.100(d), or a money transmitter, as defined in 31 CFR 1010.100(ff)(5), with a branch, subsidiary, or office located in the Covered Geographic Area," which the order defines as "Hennepin County and Ramsey County, Minnesota." A Covered Transaction is a funds transfer of $3,000 or more where the originator or transmittor provides an address in the covered area, is not publicly traded on an SEC-regulated exchange, is not a financial institution subject to Bank Secrecy Act anti-money-laundering program requirements, and where "[e]ither the beneficiary or recipient is located outside of the United States or the financial institution used by the beneficiary or recipient to receive the funds is located outside of the United States." Money transmitters must report the recipient's name, address, date of birth, phone number and email address; whether the transmittal was sourced from currency, check, credit or debit card, or other; whether the source of funds includes payments from any federal, state or local government contract or benefit program; "The form of transmittal (wire, convertible virtual currency transmission, ledger entry, or other)"; and "If the transmittal is a ledger entry that tracks credits and debits with hawaladars located internationally, whether the money transmitter uses cash couriers to settle those debits." Reports are due "by the end of the month following the month in which the Covered Transaction took place," filed as a CSV through FinCEN's Financial Industry Portal under file type "Special Measures" with identifier FIN-65547-X3M6T. Records must be retained "for a period of five years from the last day that this Order is effective." The order states that a Covered Business and "any of its officers, directors, employees, and agents, may be liable, without limitation, for civil or criminal penalties for willfully violating any of the terms of this Order," and that it "is being publicly issued, and its terms are not confidential." The information collection carries OMB control number 1506-0056.

items.title: FTC issues a policy statement that it will not pursue disparate-impact or 'unfair discrimination' claims
items.content_text:
On August 7, 2026 the Federal Trade Commission announced "a policy statement clarifying that the Commission will not pursue claims based on disparate-impact or 'unfair discrimination' theories." Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson is quoted in the release: "Disparate-impact claims are nearly impossible to square with our colorblind Constitution. They impose liability for discrimination without any evidence that anyone intended to discriminate, which pushes businesses to make race-based decisions in order to avoid liability. The Commission never had authority to impose disparate-impact liability. Today, we announce that the Commission will never do so again." The FTC states that the policy statement follows a Presidential executive order on "Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy," and that the statement explains the Commission lacks the statutory authority to consider claims under this theory. On what remains, the release states: "The statement sets forth how the Commission will pursue discrimination claims in appropriate contexts. For example, it will continue to assert disparate-treatment claims under the Equal Credit and Opportunity Act, but it will treat Section 5 of the FTC Act as the consumer-protection statute it has always been." The FTC also states that under the new policy it reviewed past decisions based on statistical analyses designed to show disparate-impact liability and entered into agreements to modify certain compliance-related obligations for Napleton Inc., Passport Auto Group and an individual previously associated with Coulter Motor Company LLC. The release states the Commission vote authorizing the policy statement and approving the agreements was 2-0.

items.title: FTC policy statement text: the Commission will no longer pursue disparate-impact claims in any context and will bring no antidiscrimination claims under Section 5, while the statement disclaims binding effect
items.content_text:
The FTC "Policy Statement Regarding Disparate-Impact Claims and 'Unfair Discrimination' Claims," listed in the FTC Legal Library under date August 7, 2026, states in its Introduction: "The FTC has previously pursued disparate-impact claims in two contexts: under Section 5 of the FTC Act (where they have been styled as 'unfair discrimination' claims), and under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act ('ECOA'). In both instances, the FTC acted ultra vires. Section 5 contains no antidiscrimination cause of action, let alone a disparate-impact one. And while ECOA does prohibit intentional discrimination, it does not authorize disparate-impact claims." It concludes: "Accordingly, in light of (1) the FTC's lack of statutory authority to bring disparate-impact claims and (2) the fundamental legal and policy defects of disparate-impact liability laid out in President Trump's executive order, the FTC will no longer pursue disparate-impact claims in any context. In addition, because Section 5 does not create an antidiscrimination cause of action, the Commission will not bring any such claims under Section 5." The statement identifies the order as "Exec. Order No. 14281, Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy, 90 Fed. Reg. 17537 (Apr. 23, 2025)" and says it directs agencies, including the FTC, to "deprioritize enforcement of all statutes and regulations to the extent they include disparate-impact liability." On what survives, the statement says "Intentional discrimination can be combatted through traditional disparate-treatment claims, and the Commission remains firmly committed to bringing such claims where the law allows," citing a July 17, 2025 concurring statement in the Asbury Automotive Group matter (Matter No. 2223135) stating the Commission "will not hesitate to bring disparate-treatment claims under ECOA where the facts support such claims." Footnote 1 states: "This Policy Statement does not confer any rights on any person and does not operate to bind the FTC or the public. In any enforcement action, the Commission must prove the challenged act or practice violates one or more existing statutory or regulatory requirements. In addition, this Policy Statement does not preempt federal, state, or local laws. Compliance with those laws, however, will not necessarily preclude Commission law enforcement action under the FTC Act or other statutes." The same footnote records that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs designated the Policy Statement as not a "major rule" as defined by 5 U.S.C. 804(2). The quoted passages are taken from the Introduction and the opening of Part II of the document; the remainder of the document was not read.

Primary source: FTC Legal Library — Policy Statement Regarding Disparate-Impact and "Unfair Discrimination" Claims — https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/disparate-impact-unfair-discrimination-claims

items.title: Senate will not vote on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act before its August recess; Majority Leader says a vote comes when the Senate returns September 14
items.content_text:
As reported by CoinDesk on August 7, 2026, "the U.S. Senate will not vote on the crypto market structure bill before it breaks for the rest of the month," with industry participants still expecting a vote in September. CoinDesk reports that Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed through a spokesperson that there would not be a vote on the Clarity Act in August but that there would be one the following month, quoting the statement: "The Dems are insistent on no Clarity vote... I worked with sponsors of the bill. [Senator Cynthia Lummis] was great, and we're getting that queued up first thing when we come back." Per the same report, the Senate returns to Washington on September 14, 2026; its remaining scheduled business before recess is a continuing resolution to fund the federal government, a Russia sanctions bill and a group of nominations; the Clarity Act had no time agreement limiting debate; the bill would require 60 votes to advance; and the outstanding issues include an ethics provision, Agriculture Committee provisions and law-enforcement concerns. The bill, H.R. 3633, previously received independent approvals from the Senate Banking Committee and the Senate Agriculture Committee. CoinDesk credits Politico with first reporting the expected absence of a pre-recess vote.

Coverage: CoinDesk — "Senate won't vote on crypto Clarity Act before its summer break," published August 7, 2026 (media coverage; no official primary record exists for an absence of scheduled floor action) — https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/08/06/senate-won-t-vote-on-crypto-clarity-act-before-its-summer-break

items.title: CFTC proposed rule "Conflicts and Affiliations" published in the Federal Register; comments due October 5, 2026
items.content_text:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission's proposed rule "Conflicts and Affiliations" was published in the Federal Register on August 6, 2026 as document 2026-15948, RIN 3038-AF76. The published document states that the Commission "is proposing new rules and amendments to its existing regulations for futures commission merchants (‘FCMs’), swap execution facilities (‘SEFs’), designated contract markets (‘DCMs’), and derivatives clearing organizations (‘DCOs’)" and that the proposal "addresses requirements relating to financial oversight of FCMs by self-regulatory organizations (‘SROs’) and designated self-regulatory organizations (‘DSROs’), as well as disclosure requirements by FCMs regarding affiliate relationships that an FCM has with a SEF, DCM, or DCO." For SEFs, DCMs and DCOs, the document states the proposal "would also establish requirements, including conflicts of interest rules, to address those registered entities' relationships with certain affiliates, such as FCM affiliates and affiliated principal trading firms," and includes guidance on safeguards to protect the impartiality of SEFs, DCMs and DCOs, addressing "the sharing of resources including staffing, technology, and office space, and limitations on the sharing of non-public information." The DATES section states: "Comments must be in writing and received by October 5, 2026." Comments are to be identified by "Conflicts and Affiliations" and RIN 3038-AF76.

items.title: Novig sues New York Attorney General and Gaming Commission in federal court over event-contract trading
items.content_text:
Ludlow Exchange, LLC d/b/a Novig filed a complaint for declaratory and injunctive relief in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York on August 5, 2026 (Case 1:26-cv-06676, Document 3) against New York Attorney General Letitia James, New York State Gaming Commission Executive Director Robert Williams, Chair Brian O'Dwyer, and the Commission's commissioners, each sued in an official capacity. The complaint states that Novig "brings this action to enjoin Defendants from enforcing New York's preempted gambling and sports wagering laws to federally regulated transactions that Congress placed within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission," and that "New York has moved aggressively against federally regulated event-contract trading within its borders, suing both KalshiEX LLC and Coinbase Financial Markets, Inc. under Executive Law Section 63(12) for offering the type of contracts at issue here." It further states that the CFTC designated Novig a Designated Contract Market on June 16, 2026, and that Novig "began offering these event contracts to customers located in New York today." The filed document was retrieved; pages 1 through 5 of 45 were read.

items.title: NYDFS settles with money transmitter Order Express for $250,000 over cybersecurity regulation violations
items.content_text:
The New York State Department of Financial Services announced on August 5, 2026 that Order Express, Inc., a licensed money transmitter, will pay a $250,000 penalty for violations of the Department's cybersecurity regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 500. According to the Department, its investigators identified deficiencies in the company's cybersecurity program and controls required under the regulation, including a failure to maintain adequate cybersecurity policies for system updates and inadequate risk assessments. The Department states that Order Express has remediated the deficiencies identified by the investigation, and that based on its limited revenue Order Express is exempt from many of Part 500's requirements. The announcement notes that the Part 500 regulation took effect in March 2017 with an amendment effective November 2023.

items.title: SDNY indicts NFT startup founder for securities and wire fraud over a $10 million SAFT raise
items.content_text:
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced on August 5, 2026 (Press Release 26-231) that Taj Tarsha, founder of Few and Far Limited, "has been indicted for securities and wire fraud for defrauding investors of the crypto startup he founded by making false and misleading statements regarding the use of investor funds and subsequently misappropriating those funds." According to the release, beginning in February 2022 Tarsha solicited investments through Simple Agreements for Future Tokens (SAFTs), under which investors paid upfront for rights to receive FAR tokens at a later date, and "raised over $10 million from the sale of 95 million FAR tokens to at least 67 investors." The offering materials promised that funds would be used to advance development of a decentralized marketplace for non-fungible tokens. The release states that "almost immediately" Tarsha began misappropriating investor funds for personal use "including gambling at an online casino and purchasing speculative cryptocurrencies," that a June 2023 audit uncovered the misappropriation, and that when the FAR token launched in May 2024 "it was effectively worthless and soon ceased trading." Tarsha, 34, of Miami, Florida, was arrested on June 6, 2026; the case is assigned to U.S. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan; each charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. The Office states that "the charges contained in the Indictment are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty."

Primary source: U.S. Department of Justice — U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, Press Release 26-231, August 5, 2026 — https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/nft-startup-founder-charged-fraud

items.title: Treasury publishes U.S.-UK Financial Regulatory Working Group joint statement recording US update on GENIUS Act stablecoin implementation
items.content_text:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury published on August 4, 2026 the joint statement of the 13th meeting of the UK-U.S. Financial Regulatory Working Group, hosted by HM Treasury in London on July 8, 2026. The statement records that U.S. Treasury and HM Treasury officials were joined by representatives of the Bank of England, the Financial Conduct Authority, the Federal Reserve Board, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission. It states that authorities provided updates on their respective regulatory regimes for digital assets, including stablecoins, and on their work to modernize payment services more broadly, and that U.S. authorities provided an update on implementing the GENIUS Act for stablecoins and on digital asset market structure. items.title: FinCEN assesses a $125 million penalty against UBS Financial Services for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations, its largest ever against a broker-dealer
items.content_text:
On August 3, 2026 the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network assessed a $125,000,000 civil money penalty against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBSFS) for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. FinCEN states this is the largest penalty ever imposed against a broker-dealer for BSA violations to date, and that it is FinCEN's second enforcement action against UBSFS after a December 2018 consent order carrying a $14.5 million penalty that had also found UBSFS failed to adequately monitor foreign currency wires. FinCEN states that despite assurances it would remediate, UBSFS did not, and subsequently failed to appropriately monitor over 50,000 foreign currency wires with an aggregate value of more than $10 billion, and did not disclose these failings to FinCEN, which learned of them through an investigation opened after a regulatory examination. FinCEN also found failures to perform appropriate customer due diligence for high-risk customers with ties to Russia and Latin America, resulting in a failure to timely report hundreds of suspicious transactions. As part of the resolution UBSFS admits it willfully violated the BSA, including failing to implement and maintain an AML program and to file suspicious activity reports. The consent order requires UBSFS to work with a third party to complete a lookback for undetected suspicious transactions and to undergo an independent review of its AML program covering priority illicit finance risks that FinCEN identifies as the U.S. Southwest border, cartels and possible narcotics trafficking, Iran, Russia and Venezuela. FinCEN states it will waive up to $15 million for expenses incurred on that undertaking upon satisfactory completion. FinCEN states that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission and FINRA cooperated on the matter.

items.title: SEC censures UBS Financial Services and imposes a $20 million penalty for failing to timely file suspicious activity reports on foreign currency wires
items.content_text:
On August 3, 2026 the Securities and Exchange Commission instituted and settled administrative and cease-and-desist proceedings against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBSFS) in Release No. 34-106026 and Advisers Act Release No. IA-6985, File No. 3-22665. The Commission found that UBSFS willfully violated Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17a-8 thereunder by failing to timely file certain suspicious activity reports. The order finds that from January 2019 through June 2023 UBSFS failed to adequately monitor customers' foreign currency wire transactions as required by its own anti-money laundering policies, because of flaws first in its legacy monitoring system and then in the automated system that replaced it in February 2021, and that UBSFS also failed to appropriately maintain customer risk profiles including red flags tied to high-risk jurisdictions. The order states that from January 2019 through January 2021 UBSFS failed to adequately monitor approximately 52,000 foreign currency wire transactions with a notional value of approximately $7.6 billion, and that from February 2021 through June 2023 it failed to monitor or adequately monitor more than 8,000 of approximately 190,000 such transactions, being 4 percent by count and carrying a notional value of more than $2.7 billion, being 20 percent by value. Lookback reports filed beginning in October 2023 were not timely under the SAR rule and concerned thousands of suspicious transactions totalling approximately $250 million. The Commission ordered UBSFS to cease and desist, censured it, and ordered payment of a $20 million civil money penalty within 30 days. UBSFS consented without admitting the findings, except as to admissions contained in its consent to the FinCEN assessment.

items.title: CFTC orders UBS Financial Services to pay $8 million for failing to diligently supervise AML transaction monitoring of foreign currency wires
items.content_text:
On August 3, 2026 the Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced, as Release 9277-26, a settled order against UBS Financial Services Inc. (UBS FSI) in CFTC Docket No. 26-04, dated July 31, 2026. The Commission found that from January 2019 through June 2023 UBS FSI, a registered futures commission merchant, failed to adequately configure and administer its anti-money laundering transaction monitoring systems for wire transfers denominated in foreign currencies and effectuated through retail customer accounts, and thereby failed to diligently supervise its business in violation of Commission Regulation 166.3. The order states that UBS FSI estimates more than 28,000 such wires with a total U.S. dollar value of at least $8.9 billion were insufficiently monitored or omitted from monitoring. It records that a manually generated report used until February 2021 did not capture scenarios such as transfers to or from high-risk jurisdictions, round dollar transactions and dormant account activity; that a coding error discovered in October 2020 had suppressed more than 400 alerts; and that after the automated system went live in March 2021 the firm configured it to draw on an intra-day feed rather than a complete end-of-day feed and did not remediate that and a transaction-labelling issue until October 2022. The order states that a violation of Regulation 166.3 is an independent violation for which no underlying violation is necessary. UBS FSI submitted an offer of settlement, admits the facts set out in the order and acknowledges that its conduct violated Regulation 166.3. The order requires UBS FSI to cease and desist and to pay an $8,000,000 civil monetary penalty within thirty days, and imposes cooperation undertakings. The CFTC release states that FinCEN, the SEC and FINRA announced related actions against UBS FSI the same day.

items.title: New York sues KalshiEX, LLC in state court, alleging its prediction market is an unlicensed gambling operation
items.content_text:
On July 31, 2026, New York Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James announced that New York has sued KalshiEX, LLC for running an illegal gambling operation in New York through its prediction market platform. The Office of the Attorney General states that its investigation found Kalshi's prediction market is an illegal, unlicensed gambling operation, and that the lawsuit alleges Kalshi's prediction markets meet the legal definition of gambling because the outcomes of the events users bet on are uncertain and outside the control of the bettor or hinge on a game of chance. The Attorney General is asking the court to order Kalshi to stop operating as an unlicensed gambling business, forfeit all illegal gains, distribute restitution to consumers who were harmed, and pay fines equal to three times the gains the company made. items.title: CFTC settles manipulation charges over trading of a State of the Union event contract, with $17,569.98 disgorgement, a $17,500 penalty and a three-year trading ban
items.content_text:
On July 31, 2026 the Commodity Futures Trading Commission entered a settled Order Instituting Proceedings under Section 6(c) and (d) of the Commodity Exchange Act against George Anthony Devolder Santos, CFTC Docket No. 26-05, announced as CFTC Release 9276-26. The Commission found that between February 12, 2026 and February 25, 2026 Santos violated Section 6(c)(1) of the Act, 7 U.S.C. 9(1), and Regulation 180.1(a)(1), (3). The order states that KalshiEX LLC, a designated contract market, offered an event contract titled "Who will attend the State of the Union?" and a market on whether Santos would attend the 2026 State of the Union, and that Santos traded both Yes and No positions in that market while making social media statements about his attendance, exiting the No position on February 25 for a profit of $14,390.57. The order states that event contracts are a type of swap as defined by the Act, and that Santos violated Section 6(c)(1) and Regulation 180.1(a) when he traded in an event contract where he could influence the outcome of the underlying event and engaged in activity designed to affect the price of the swap. Santos consented to the order without admitting the findings or conclusions. The order requires him to cease and desist, to disgorge $17,569.98, to pay a $17,500 civil monetary penalty within thirty days, and prohibits him from trading on or subject to the rules of any registered entity for three years. KalshiEX LLC is identified in the order as the venue that listed the contract and is not a respondent.

items.title: SEC approves amended generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares, adding a 15% digital-commodity buffer and allowing actively managed products
items.content_text:
In three orders published in the Federal Register between July 30 and August 3, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission approved amendments to the generic listing standards for Commodity-Based Trust Shares at Nasdaq, NYSE Arca and Cboe BZX. In Release No. 34-105995 (July 27, 2026; File No. SR-NASDAQ-2026-032), the Commission approved new Nasdaq Rule 5711(d)(iv)(C), which provides that up to 15 percent of a Commodity-Based Trust Share's net asset value in the aggregate may consist of digital commodities that do not meet the existing criteria for commodities, or securities that do not meet the existing criteria for securities, with any derivative calculated on its gross notional value. The rule defines 'digital commodity' to mean a commodity that is a digital asset and is intrinsically linked to and derives its value from the programmatic operation of a functional crypto system, as well as supply and demand dynamics, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others. The exchanges state that this definition is informed by the joint interpretive guidance issued by the Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission published at 91 FR 13714 on March 23, 2026, and that each exchange will submit a rule filing to conform the definition if legislation is enacted defining the term. The same orders remove the requirement that Commodity-Based Trust Shares be designed to reflect the performance of one or more reference assets or an index of reference assets, which permits actively managed products to be listed under the generic standards, and add a trading-halt requirement where portfolio information is not disseminated to all market participants at the same time, together with a requirement that persons with access to non-public portfolio information be subject to procedures designed to prevent its use and dissemination. At least 85 percent of net asset value must remain in assets already permitted under the standards, and the Cboe BZX order states that the sponsor must monitor compliance with the 85 percent threshold daily and promptly notify the exchange of any breach. The companion orders are Release No. 34-106001 (July 28, 2026; File No. SR-NYSEARCA-2026-42), amending NYSE Arca Rule 8.201-E (Generic), and Release No. 34-106011 (July 29, 2026; File No. SR-CboeBZX-2026-061), amending Cboe BZX Rule 14.11(e)(4).

items.title: CFTC staff advisory warns designated contract markets against broad, template-style self-certifications of event contract series
items.content_text:
On July 24, 2026, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission's Division of Market Oversight (DMO) issued an advisory reminding designated contract markets (DCMs) about the proper procedures for submitting self-certifications of an event contract series. The advisory addresses concerns about the practice of submitting broad, template-style certifications that combine many potential event contract variations into a single certification. According to the advisory, this approach limits DMO's ability to determine whether a DCM has provided all the information, explanation, and analysis required by Commission Regulation Section 40.2, and whether it has adequately evaluated the settlement methodology, data sources, and core-principles compliance of any contract it intends to list. The guidance reiterates that broad, template-style certifications should not be submitted, and explains when closely related event contracts may be certified as a class or submitted for approval under Commission Regulations Sections 40.2(d) or 40.3. items.title: Reported: New would-be-final CLARITY Act draft circulated July 22 with DOJ-enforced ethics ban on federal officials issuing digital assets

As reported by CoinDesk on July 22, 2026 and corroborated by CNBC, Roll Call, American Banker and Disruption Banking the same day, lawmakers circulated a would-be-final draft of the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act as the U.S. Senate prepared for floor action before its August recess. items.title: Washington State Court Grants Preliminary Injunction Against Kalshi for Violations of State Gambling Act and Consumer Protection Act
items.content_text:
King County Superior Court (Washington state) granted a preliminary injunction against Kalshi on July 20, 2026, finding that Kalshi's prediction market contracts likely violate both the Washington Gambling Act and the Consumer Protection Act. Washington AG Nick Brown filed the underlying complaint on March 27, 2026. The court will issue a final injunction order setting full remedies on August 5, 2026. items.title: Fed Chair Warsh testifies to House Financial Services: no Federal Reserve bailout for crypto or stablecoins; Fed 'racing' to meet GENIUS Act stablecoin rulemaking deadline; nonbank fintech payment access pressed
items.content_text:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh testified before the House Committee on Financial Services on July 14, 2026, as part of the Semiannual Monetary Policy Report (2128 Rayburn House Office Building, 10:00 AM). The official prepared statement focused on price stability, monetary policy, and internal Fed task forces. During the Q&A, Warsh made three statements directly relevant to crypto, stablecoin, and fintech operators: (1) No Federal Reserve bailout for crypto or stablecoins: Pressed by Rep. Brad Sherman on whether the Fed would provide the kind of support it gave money market funds in 2008, Warsh stated 'We do not want to be in the bailout business, full stop.' He added that the Fed would 'do everything we can to mitigate... extraordinary risks' but would not bail out crypto. He did not fully rule out marginal systemic-spillover mitigation. (2) GENIUS Act rulemaking urgency: Warsh told lawmakers the Fed is 'racing' to finalize its portion of the GENIUS Act stablecoin implementing rules ahead of the July 18, 2026 one-year statutory deadline. The deadline has since been confirmed missed (the Federal Register contains no in-scope publication; July 18 is a Saturday; earliest possible publication is Monday July 20). (3) Nonbank fintech payment-system access: Rep. Sherman separately pressed on Kraken's pending bank application and nonbank crypto firms seeking direct access to the payment system; Warsh invoked systemic-risk considerations without making a specific commitment. Background: Warsh is the most crypto-sympathetic Fed Chair on record, having previously disclosed venture stakes in Bitcoin payments, a crypto index manager, Bitwise, and a stablecoin venture â all divested under Fed ethics rules prior to confirmation in May 2026. items.title: Arizona Department of Gaming issues cease-and-desist orders to five online gambling operators alleging felony promotion of gambling, illegal control of an enterprise, and money laundering
items.content_text:
On July 10, 2026, the Arizona Department of Gaming announced it had issued cease-and-desist orders to BetOpenly, Bookmaker, Club WPT Online Poker, Kutt Inc., and Raffle Creator, with each enforcement action alleging conduct giving rise to the felonies of promotion of gambling, illegal control of an enterprise, and money laundering. Notified entities are directed to immediately stop all gambling operations and activities in Arizona and to desist from future illegal gambling operations; the Department states future actions may include criminal charges or civil action against entities, principals, and employees, potential restitution awards, and forfeiture of all monies acquired due to the illegal conduct. Department Director Jackie Johnson said, 'Through these cease-and-desist orders we are putting operators on notice: their conduct runs contrary to Arizona law and they must stop promoting illegal gambling.' items.title: SCOTUS rules 6-3 that for-cause removal protections for SEC and CFTC commissioners are unconstitutional (Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332)
items.content_text:
On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court of the United States issued its 6-3 opinion in Trump v. Slaughter (No. 25-332), authored by Chief Justice Roberts, overturning Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935). The Court held that the for-cause removal protection in the FTC's enabling statute — and by structural extension the SEC and CFTC, which operate under identical removal provisions — is contrary to the separation of powers under the Constitution. Effective immediately, the President may remove SEC and CFTC commissioners without cause. A companion order in Trump v. Cook (No. 25A312, June 29, 2026) denied a government application to stay a preliminary injunction protecting Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook; the Federal Reserve's statutory structure was not directly addressed by the majority opinion. The opinion is published on the Court's official slip opinion list for October Term 2025.

items.title: CFTC sues New Mexico over prediction-market preemption (8th state)
items.content_text:
On 2026-06-12 the CFTC filed suit against the State of New Mexico, seeking a declaratory judgment that federal law grants it exclusive authority over event contracts and a permanent injunction barring the state from enforcing preempted gaming laws against CFTC registrants. New Mexico joins AZ, CT, IL, NY, MN, RI, and WI.
